h1: Starting a gin brand: distil it yourself or contract it
title: Distil or Contract Your Gin Brand | Craft Beer School
desc: The real trade-offs between building your own still and having a distillery make your gin, with the questions to settle before you spend anything.
teaser: Own still or someone else's? The answer decides your capital, your control and your story.
standfirst: Every gin founder meets this fork early. One road starts with a still and a licence. The other starts with a recipe and a contract. Here is how to choose with your eyes open.
sections: Two ways into the same bottle

Gin is a neutral spirit flavoured predominantly with juniper. How you reach that spirit and those flavours is where the business models split.

A distilling brand owns or rents the still, buys neutral spirit and redistils it with botanicals. A contract brand designs the recipe and the identity, then pays an existing distillery to make the gin to specification. Many brands begin as the second and move to the first. Some stay contract for good and are perfectly healthy.

Neither road is the serious one. The question is which risks you would rather carry in the first two years.
What distilling yourself asks of you

A still is the visible part. Behind it sit premises that meet the rules of your state or country, a licence for manufacture and a safe way of handling ethanol. You also need water, power and people who can run a batch the same way every time.

You also take on the learning. Cutting heads from hearts from tails, managing botanical loading and judging a distillate are skills built over many runs, not one weekend. Our gin distillery business plan guide lists what a lender or partner will expect to see before you commit.

The upside is control. You can change a recipe, run a small experimental batch and show visitors where the gin comes from. If you plan other spirits later, the same equipment can often be reused.

Contract production moves the capital and much of the licensing weight to the distillery. You still need a brand owner's approvals, label registration and a route to market. Read how contract-distilled gin works before you sign anything.

The trade is dependence. Your batch slot, your minimum run size and your recipe confidentiality all sit with someone else. If the distillery changes its terms or its neutral spirit supplier, you feel it. A good agreement says who owns the recipe, who owns the botanical stock and what happens if either side walks away.

Be honest in the story, too. A brand can say its gin is made by a partner distillery. It should not suggest a copper still it does not own. Our guide on a gin brand story that is true covers this.
A way to compare the two

Put both on one page, using your own quotes rather than guesses:

  • Money before the first sale: equipment, premises, licence work, stock, deposits.
  • Cost per bottle at your expected volume (see working out the cost of a bottle).
  • Time to the first legal sale, which depends on your jurisdiction and its licensing queue.
  • Control: recipe changes, batch size, quality checks.
  • Risk: a bad batch, a supplier failure, a partner who moves on.

Whichever column wins, check it against cash. A model that works on paper but needs more working capital than you can raise is not a plan.
Questions to settle before you choose

• Do you want to be a producer or a brand builder? Both are real jobs. They use different skills.
  • How many bottles do you expect in year one? Can you say why?
  • Will you sell to a state or country where alcohol is tightly regulated? Check the licensing route first, because it can decide the whole structure. Alcohol is a state subject in India, so rules and timelines differ from state to state.
  • Who will taste every batch and have the authority to reject it?

A brewer's habit helps here. Decide on the quality bar before the first batch exists, then build the process to meet it.
The middle path: rent time on someone else's still

Between the two roads sits a third. Some distilleries let a brand owner run their own batches on the host's equipment, with the host's staff or under their supervision. You learn the craft without buying the plant.

This can suit a founder who wants to understand distillation properly. You see how the cuts behave, how botanical loading changes the aroma and how a recipe scales from a trial to a full run. Ask any host the same questions you would ask a contract partner: who owns the recipe, who owns leftover botanicals and who holds the licences.
How the choice shows up in your cash

Distilling yourself front-loads cash into equipment, premises and licence work, then lowers the cost of each extra bottle once the plant is busy. Contracting spreads cost across each run, so cash goes out as you produce.

Neither is automatically cheaper. A still that sits idle three days out of five carries its cost anyway. A contract fee that looks high per bottle may still win when your volume is small. Draw a month-by-month cash line for each option for the first two years and see where each one runs lowest.

If you have little capital and no distilling experience, a contract trial run teaches you a great deal about recipe, price and market for a small outlay. If you already have premises, partners and a plan for several spirits, a still may make sense from day one.

Either way, write the numbers down. A written plan exposes the weak assumption while it is still cheap to change.
faqs: Yes, if it meets the legal definition of gin where it is sold. The category depends on how the spirit is made and flavoured, not on who owns the still.
Can I switch from contract to my own still later?
Many brands do. Keep your recipe and your specifications in your own hands from the start, so the move changes the maker and not the gin.
Contracting usually needs less capital up front. Your cost per bottle may be higher, so work out both at your expected volume before you decide.
Do I need a licence if a distillery makes my gin?
Often yes, for the brand owner, labels and sales. Rules differ by country and by Indian state and they change, so check with your regulator or a licensing adviser.
